title: The Artin Action on a Free Group

items.title: Standard meridians of a punctured disk
items.statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$, let $D^2=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|\le1\}$ and
$Q_n=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the closed unit disk and the base configuration of
[[def-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-a-punctured-disk]], so that
$q_1<\dots<q_n$ are distinct points of the real axis of
$\operatorname{int}D^2$. Fix the boundary basepoint
$$d:=(0,1)\in\partial D^2 .$$
For $1\le i\le n$ let $s_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2$ be the **straight stem**
$$s_i(t):=(1-t)\,d+t\,q_i ,$$
the straight segment from $d$ to $q_i$, and choose a round circle $C_i$ in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ centred at $q_i$, of radius $0<\varepsilon_i<d(q_i,\partial D^2)$
so small that the closed disks $B_i$ bounded by the circles are pairwise disjoint, that each circle meets only its own stem, and that it meets $s_i$ exactly once, at
$p_i:=s_i(1-\varepsilon_i/L_i)$ where $L_i:=|d-q_i|$, and meets no other stem
$s_j$ with $j\ne i$. Write $c_i\colon[0,1]\to D^2\setminus Q_n$ for $C_i$
traversed once **positively** (counterclockwise), from $p_i$ back to $p_i$.
The **standard meridian loops** are the loops based at $d$
$$x_i:=s_i\,c_i\,s_i^{-1},\qquad 1\le i\le n,$$
read as $s_i$ from $d$ to $p_i$, then $c_i$, then $s_i$ from $p_i$ back to $d$
([[def-based-loops-and-fundamental-group]]). Further, $\partial$ denotes the
**positively oriented boundary loop**
$$\partial(t):=d\,e^{2\pi i t},\qquad t\in[0,1],$$
of $D^2$ based at $d$: it traverses $\partial D^2$ once counterclockwise,
starting and ending at $d$.

**Existence and independence of the choices.** The straight segments $s_i$
leave $d$ in pairwise distinct directions (the points $q_1,\dots,q_n$ are
distinct and lie strictly below $d$) and meet one another only at $d$; the
segments $s_i$ meet the real axis only at their endpoints $q_i$. An explicit choice-free family is given by
$$\varepsilon_i=\frac14\min\left(\{1-|q_i|\}\cup\left\{|q_i-q_j|,\frac{|q_i-q_j|}{\sqrt{1+q_j^2}}:j\ne i\right\}\right).$$
The finite set inside the minimum is nonempty and contains only positive
numbers. The distance from $q_i$ to the line through $d,q_j$ is
$|q_i-q_j|/\sqrt{1+q_j^2}$, so $B_i$ misses every other stem. Also
$\varepsilon_i+\varepsilon_j\le|q_i-q_j|/2<|q_i-q_j|$, proving disjointness
of the **closed** disks, and $\varepsilon_i<1-|q_i|$ keeps each disk inside
$D^2$. The radius is less than $|d-q_i|$, giving exactly the displayed contact
with its own stem. For $n=1$ the minimum has only its boundary-margin entry;
for $n=0$ the family is empty. Any family satisfying these conditions may be
fixed; this formula witnesses its existence without any choice axiom.

The class $[x_i]\in\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ is independent of
all admissible radii, including the old broader convention requiring only
avoidance of the other stems. Such a circle encloses no $q_j$ with $j\ne i$:
otherwise the other stem from $d$, which lies outside the circle, to $q_j$
would cross it (or have $q_j$ on it). Thus the larger disk of any two admissible
concentric circles still contains no other puncture. Interpolate their radii
and their tether contact points radially; this is a based lasso homotopy in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$ ([[def-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy]]).
It does not require the intermediate circle to be disjoint from the other
circles, so the class argument does not circularly assume the newly explicit
representative convention. Fix once and
for all one such family of circles; every statement on this page uses that
fixed family.

**Frozen conventions of the page.** The stems and the basepoint transport are
fixed once and for all by the choices above; the stems are indexed so that the
positively oriented boundary loop $\partial$, as seen from $d$, meets the
directions of the stems in the order $s_1,s_2,\dots,s_n$; and every braid word
is read left-to-right and acts by composition of the corresponding
automorphisms. No relation of the braid presentation and no choice principle
is used in this definition.
items.proof_strategy: The straight segments from $d$ to the distinct points $q_i$ of the real axis leave $d$ in distinct directions and otherwise meet only in $d$, and small round circles around distinct points are pairwise disjoint; choose the radii so small that $C_i$ meets only $s_i$ and no other stem. Hence the displayed loops exist and are unambiguous. The index convention ('boundary meets $s_1$ first') is arranged by choosing $C_i$ (not the labelling of punctures) appropriately; verify it once by tracing the counterclockwise boundary from $d=(0,1)$, which sees the directions to $q_1<\dots<q_n$ in increasing index order. Record explicitly that no relation of the presentation and no choice principle is used.

items.title: The standard flower is a deformation retract with free meridian basis
items.statement:
For each standard meridian let $t_i$ be its truncated tether from $d$ to
$p_i\in C_i$, namely the restriction of $s_i$ to
$[0,1-\varepsilon_i/|d-q_i|]$. The **standard flower** is the finite graph
$$W=\{d\}\cup\bigcup_{i=1}^n(t_i\cup C_i)\subseteq D^2\setminus Q_n.$$
Then $W$ is a deformation retract of $D^2\setminus Q_n$, fixing $d$;
$\pi_1(W,d)$ is free with basis $[x_1],\dots,[x_n]$; and
$\pi_j(W,d)=0$ for all $j\ge2$. The tethers are edges of a tree, not parts
of embedded circle summands through $d$.
items.proof_strategy: Radially evacuate each deleted puncture neighborhood onto its small boundary circle. Polygonize the compact holed disk with tether-fixing collars: near d use width |x|/2 and the bound y<=1-|x|. Cut along the finite tether tree to obtain a disk; retract that disk onto its complementary boundary arc while fixing all paired shores, then descend the homotopy to the compact flower. Collapse the tether tree by the based CW-subcomplex equivalence to get a genuine wedge of circles and its free meridian basis. Its reduced-word covering tree contracts, so based sphere lifting gives vanishing higher homotopy. For n=0 use the straight-line contraction to d. No AC is consumed.

items.title: The punctured-disk fundamental group is free on the standard meridians
items.statement: Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of [[def-free-group]] on $n$ letters. The assignment $x_i\mapsto[x_i]$ extends to a group isomorphism $F_n\to\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$; equivalently, the classes $[x_1],\dots,[x_n]$ of the standard meridians of [[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]] form a free basis of $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$.
items.proof_strategy: By clause (i) of the flower lemma, inclusion followed by the retraction induces mutually inverse isomorphisms between $\pi_1(W,d)$ and $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$; clause (ii) identifies $\pi_1(W,d)$ as free on the classes of the $x_i$. Compose with the canonical isomorphism from the free group on the letters $x_i$ (universal property of [[def-free-group]], uniqueness as in [[thm-free-groups-unique-up-to-unique-isomorphism]]). The case $n=0$ is included: then $D^2$ is contractible and the basis is empty.

items.title: The standard stem system cuts the punctured disk open to a disk
items.statement:
Assume AC. Cutting $D^2\setminus Q_n$ open along the standard stem system
$s_1,\dots,s_n$ of [[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]], **with each
puncture end completed by its slit-tip point**, yields a compact connected
surface $H$ homeomorphic to the closed disk $D^2$. Each slit has two boundary
sides meeting at its puncture tip; the outer boundary is opened at $d$ into
boundary arcs. A homeomorphism of $D^2$ fixing $\partial D^2$, $Q_n$, and
all the stems pointwise lifts to a homeomorphism of $H$ fixing $\partial H$
pointwise, and conversely such a homeomorphism of $H$ reglues to a
homeomorphism of $D^2$.
items.proof_strategy: Model $H$ explicitly: in polar coordinates around $d$ the slit star opens to a curvilinear polygon in the plane whose boundary is a simple closed curve made of the outer arc, the $2n$ slit sides and the $n$ puncture corners, so by the Jordan-Schoenflies extension for plane curves ([[lem-jordan-schoenflies-extension-for-plane-curves]], which uses the stated AC) the closed bounded Jordan region it bounds is a closed disk and $H\cong D^2$. Record the boundary bookkeeping of the model: the $n$ slits contribute $2n$ boundary arcs, each puncture $q_i$ is the corner where the two sides of $s_i$ meet, and the outer circle contributes one arc whose endpoints are the two sides of the opened basepoint $d$; the result is compact, connected, with exactly one boundary circle. The descent/reglue sentence is the standard one for maps fixing the cuts: a homeomorphism of $D^2$ fixing $\partial D^2$, $Q_n$ and each $s_i$ pointwise induces a homeomorphism of $H$ fixing $\partial H$ pointwise, and conversely such a homeomorphism of $H$ reglues to one of $D^2$; no other choice is used.

items.title: The oriented boundary loop represents the ordered product of the standard meridians
items.statement: With the conventions of [[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]], the positively oriented boundary loop $\partial$ represents the ordered product of the standard meridians in $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$: $[\partial]=[x_1][x_2]\cdots[x_n]$.
items.proof_strategy: Construct the compact cut disk locally, using tether-disjoint circle collars, polygonal boundaries and the finite vertex-sector/edge-strip construction of [[lem-finite-polygonal-disk-and-collar-surgery]]. Its two boundary paths A and P have the same sector endpoints and are homotopic relative to those endpoints in a convex disk coordinate. After regluing, A is the positive outer boundary and P traverses each tether out, its inner circle counterclockwise, and its tether back, in the frozen increasing order. Thus the boundary class is [x_1]...[x_n]. For n=0 contract the boundary by straight-line interpolation to d. All constructions are finite and choice-free; the flower Statement is used only for its tether-tree geometry.

items.title: A based self-map of the punctured disk inducing the identity on the fundamental group is based-homotopic to the identity
items.statement: Let $f:D^2\setminus Q_n\to D^2\setminus Q_n$ be continuous with $f(d)=d$ and $f_*=\mathrm{id}$ on $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$. Then $f$ is homotopic to the identity relative to $d$. No choice principle is used.
items.proof_strategy: Use the based flower retraction and the based tether-tree collapse to obtain inverse equivalences a:X->R and b:R->X with R a genuine finite wedge of circles. For g=afb, identity induced action fixes each standard generator-loop class; finitely many based loop homotopies glue on R to g homotopic to its identity. Transport this homotopy along a,b to f homotopic to the identity relative to d. The flower is a lollipop graph, not a wedge homeomorphism. The case n=0 is the based disk contraction; no extension to a puncture or choice principle is claimed.

items.title: Plane arc extension and rectangular neighborhoods
items.statement:
Assume AC. If $a:[0,1]\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is an embedding, there is a
plane homeomorphism $G$ with $G(a(t))=(t,0)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$.
Consequently the arc has a rectangular neighborhood along its interior and
half-rectangle sector neighborhoods at its endpoints, obtained by transporting
those neighborhoods of the straight interval.
items.proof_strategy: Normalize endpoints, lift under z^2 to a Jordan curve; prove complementary component exchange by relative homology; extend one half equivariantly using relative Schoenflies; descend and normalize the plane point.

items.title: Homotopic simple proper arcs in the punctured disk are isotopic relative to their endpoints
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $\alpha,\beta$ be simple proper arcs in the punctured disk with the same
endpoints, each on $\partial D^2$ or at a puncture, homotopic relative to
endpoints through proper arcs. Then they are isotopic relative to endpoints as unoriented arc images. For distinct ordered endpoints their given parametrizations can also be joined by an isotopy of parametrized arcs.
Here an arc with a puncture endpoint is understood via its continuous extension
to $[0,1]$ in the filled disk; the homotopy is continuous on $[0,1]\times I$
there, its endpoints are fixed, and its interior avoids $Q_n\cup\partial D^2$.
Restricting away from a puncture endpoint gives the proper arc in
$D^2\setminus Q_n$.
items.proof_strategy: Use the bigon criterion for arcs (Farb-Margalit, A Primer on Mapping Class Groups, Proposition 1.7 and the arc discussion in section 1.2.7, printed pp. 31 and 37-38): two simple proper arcs in minimal position, considered up to isotopy relative to their endpoints, are isotopic if and only if they do not cobound a bigon or half-bigon. Put $\alpha,\beta$ in minimal position relative to the endpoints (finitely many transverse intersections by compactness), remove bigons one at a time by an isotopy fixing the endpoints, and iterate; the half-bigon obstruction described in the source is exactly what is excluded by restricting to isotopies relative to the boundary/endpoints. Conclude that homotopy rel endpoints implies isotopy rel endpoints. Record that only finitely many bigons arise and that each removal strictly decreases the number of interior intersections, so the process terminates.

items.title: Smooth relative isotopy extension for disk arcs with puncture endpoints
items.statement: Assume the countable axiom of choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $F:[0,1]\times[0,1]\to D^2$ be a smooth map such that: (1) for every $s$, the map $u\mapsto F(u,s)$ is a smooth embedding of $[0,1]$ with fixed endpoints $p_0:=F(0,0)$, $p_1:=F(1,0)$ that lie either on $\partial D^2$ or in a finite set $P\subseteq\operatorname{int}D^2$, with the interiors of the arcs inside $\operatorname{int}D^2$; (2) the isotopy is stationary on collars of its endpoints; (3) the moving part avoids $P$ and a closed set $C\subseteq D^2$. Then there is a smooth ambient isotopy $\Phi:D^2\times[0,1]\to D^2$ with $\Phi_0=\mathrm{id}$, each $\Phi_s$ a homeomorphism fixing $\partial D^2$, $P$ and $C$ pointwise, and $\Phi_s(F(u,0))=F(u,s)$ for all $u,s$; the finite-sequence clause of the published lemma carries over verbatim.
items.proof_strategy: Repeat the flow construction of the published boundary-endpoint lemma: extend the arc track to an embedded surface in space-time, extend the velocity field along it, cut it off near $(\partial D^2\cup P\cup C)\times[0,1]$, and flow. The only change is that an endpoint may lie in $P$: the endpoint track is the constant point $p_1$ (by the stationary-collar hypothesis), the velocity vanishes there, and the cut-off neighbourhood of the moving part avoids $(\partial D^2\cup P\cup C)\times[0,1]$, so uniqueness of the flow equation still fixes the endpoint and each set pointwise. Verify explicitly that the published argument's compactness and cut-off steps (its steps 1.1-2.2) are unchanged; the finite-sequence clause is proved exactly as there.

items.title: Trivial action on the standard meridians fixes the punctures and the stem arcs up to homotopy
items.statement:
Let $h\in\operatorname{Homeo}^+(D^2,\partial D^2)$ preserve $Q_n$ setwise
and induce the identity on $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$. Then $h(q_i)=q_i$
for every $i$, and $h(s_i)$ is homotopic to $s_i$
relative to endpoints. Relative homotopy uses continuous maps of the compact
parameter square into the filled disk, with fixed endpoints $d,q_i$ and
all other arc points avoiding $Q_n$. No choice principle is used.
items.proof_strategy: (1) Let $\sigma$ be the permutation with $h(q_i)=q_{\sigma(i)}$. Then $h(x_i)=h(s_i)\,c'_{\sigma(i)}\,h(s_i)^{-1}$ for a positively oriented small circle around $q_{\sigma(i)}$, so $[x_i]=h_*[x_i]$ is conjugate to $[x_{\sigma(i)}]^{\pm1}$; apply the homomorphism $F_n\to\mathbb Z$ sending $x_k\mapsto\delta_{ik}$ (well defined by the universal property of [[def-free-group]]) to both sides to get $\sigma(i)=i$ and the plus sign, using the free basis of the fundamental-group theorem. (2) By the based-map lemma $h\simeq\mathrm{id}_X$ rel $d$; the tracks $t\mapsto H_t\circ s_i$ of the stems are a homotopy of proper arcs. Justify that the tracked end remains $q_i$ throughout: the end of a proper arc depends locally constantly on the homotopy parameter, and the space of punctures is discrete, so the end cannot jump (crucially $h(q_i)=q_i$). Hence $h(s_i)$ and $s_i$ are homotopic through proper arcs with the same endpoints, and the homotopy is upgraded to an isotopy rel endpoints by the arc-isotopy criterion. Note for Step 3: the two displayed inputs ((1) conjugacy comparison, (2) end-continuity of the homotopy tracks) are the delicate points of this item and must both be written out.

items.title: A standard stem arc system can be straightened by a boundary- and puncture-fixed ambient isotopy
items.statement:
Assume AC. Let $h\in\operatorname{Homeo}^+(D^2,\partial D^2)$ fix every
$q_i$, and suppose each $h(s_i)$ is isotopic to $s_i$ relative to endpoints.
Then $h$ is isotopic relative to $\partial D^2\cup Q_n$ to a homeomorphism
$h'$ with $h'(s_i(t))=s_i(t)$ for every $i,t$.
items.proof_strategy: Replace $h$ by the smooth representative of its mapping class and its smooth isotopy from the identity supplied by part 3 of the published mapping-class theorem; smoothing the arc isotopies of the previous item is legitimate because a relative isotopy of smooth arcs can be replaced by a smooth one (flag for Step 3). Apply the puncture-endpoint extension lemma to the isotopy from $s_1$ to $h(s_1)$ with $P=Q_n$ and $C=\partial D^2$, obtaining an ambient isotopy $\Phi^{(1)}$ fixing $\partial D^2\cup Q_n$ with $\Phi^{(1)}_1(h(s_1))=s_1$. Then apply it to the composite for $s_2$, with the closed set $C$ enlarged by $s_1$ and the earlier images, and so on; the finite-sequence clause of the extension lemma glues the finitely many isotopies, and at each stage the earlier arcs, the outer boundary and every puncture remain fixed. The result is an ambient isotopy rel $\partial D^2\cup Q_n$ carrying $h$ to a homeomorphism $h'$ fixing $\bigcup_i s_i$ pointwise. AC_\omega is discharged from AC by the published implication theorem.

items.title: A boundary-fixed punctured-disk homeomorphism acting trivially on the fundamental group is isotopic to the identity
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $h\in\operatorname{Homeo}^+(D^2,\partial D^2)$ preserve $Q_n$ setwise and act as the identity on $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$. Then $h$ is isotopic to $\mathrm{id}_{D^2}$ relative to $\partial D^2$ and $Q_n$.
items.proof_strategy: Induct after filling the last puncture; transport the truncation to canonical rank using an explicit finite point motion. The independently proved point-pushing kernel theorem gives a single moving-point loop. The compact ambient tether square and the choice-free relative stem homotopy imply that loop is nullhomotopic; its point push is therefore trivial. No arc-tameness or general arc-isotopy result is needed.

items.title: Artin automorphisms of the free group
items.statement:
Let $F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of
[[def-free-group]], identified with $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ through the
standard meridians by
[[thm-the-punctured-disk-fundamental-group-is-free-on-standard-meridians]]. For
$1\le i\le n-1$, $\rho(\sigma_i)\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is the automorphism
given on the basis by
$$\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)=x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})=x_i, \qquad \rho(\sigma_i)(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
Its inverse is
$$\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_i)=x_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_{i+1})=x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1},\qquad \rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_j)=x_j\ (j\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$
This is the convention frozen for the page: braid words act from left to right
and $\rho(\sigma_i^{-1}):=\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}$.

**The assignments are automorphisms, and the displayed formulas are inverse.**
By the universal property of the free group
([[def-free-group]], [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]]) the displayed
values on the free basis extend to a unique endomorphism
$\rho(\sigma_i):F_n\to F_n$, and likewise the displayed inverse formulas extend
to an endomorphism $\theta:F_n\to F_n$. Substituting,
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_i)\bigr)=\theta(x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1}) =\theta(x_i)\,\theta(x_{i+1})\,\theta(x_i)^{-1} =x_{i+1}\,\bigl(x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}\bigr)\,x_{i+1}^{-1}=x_i,$$
$$\theta\bigl(\rho(\sigma_i)(x_{i+1})\bigr)=\theta(x_i)=x_{i+1},$$
and both composites fix every other basis element; so
$\theta\circ\rho(\sigma_i)=\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$ on a basis, hence as
endomorphisms. Symmetrically $\rho(\sigma_i)\circ\theta=
\operatorname{id}_{F_n}$. Therefore $\rho(\sigma_i)$ is a bijection with the
displayed inverse, i.e. an automorphism
([[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]).

**Convention note.** The displayed formulas are Artin's equations (14) and (15)
with the letter $\sigma_i$ and its inverse interchanged; under the frozen
geometric conventions of this library the *positive* half twist is the
anticlockwise supported half rotation (see
`def-elementary-geometric-half-twist` and
`thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk`),
and
`prop-the-geometric-action-on-meridians-is-the-artin-representation` proves
that its action on the standard meridians is exactly the substitution frozen
above. The interchange is a convention, not a change of mathematical content:
$\rho$ and Artin's substitution generate the same subgroup of
$\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ and satisfy the same braid relations, and the
companion page shows that the mirror (clockwise) half rotation realizes
Artin's displayed formulas verbatim.
items.proof_strategy: The displayed assignments on the free basis extend to endomorphisms by the universal property of the free group, and the displayed inverse formulas are verified by substituting and reducing: $\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1})=x_i$ and $\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1})=x_{i+1}$, with all other generators fixed on both sides; hence each $\rho(\sigma_i)$ is bijective. Record the two-sided verification of the inverse, that the $x_i$ denote the meridian classes under the identification theorem, and that the formulas are those of Artin (1947), equation (14) (with (15) for the inverse), and of Gonzalez-Meneses, section 1.6.

items.title: The Artin automorphisms satisfy the braid relations
items.statement: For the automorphisms of [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]]: if $|i-j|>1$ then $\rho(\sigma_i)\rho(\sigma_j)=\rho(\sigma_j)\rho(\sigma_i)$; if $|i-j|=1$ then $\rho(\sigma_i)\rho(\sigma_j)\rho(\sigma_i)=\rho(\sigma_j)\rho(\sigma_i)\rho(\sigma_j)$.
items.proof_strategy: Compute both composites on every basis element and compare reduced words. For $|i-j|>1$ the supports are disjoint or commute, so the two sides move no generator differently. For $|i-j|=1$, compute the two three-fold composites on $x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ (with all other generators fixed): both send $x_i\mapsto x_{i+2}$, $x_{i+1}\mapsto x_{i+2}^{-1}x_ix_{i+2}$, $x_{i+2}\mapsto x_{i+2}^{-1}x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}x_{i+2}$; finish with $\rho(\sigma_i)^2(x_i)=x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}$ and the corresponding adjacencies. Equality of two automorphisms is checked on the free basis (universal property).

items.title: The Artin representation on a free group
items.statement:
By [[lem-artin-automorphisms-satisfy-the-braid-relations]] the assignment
$\sigma_i\mapsto\rho(\sigma_i)$ satisfies the defining relations of the
presented braid group $B_n$ of
[[def-braid-group-by-the-artin-presentation]], so von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] yields a unique homomorphism
$$\rho:B_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(F_n).$$
This is the **Artin representation**; it is the frozen convention for every
later statement of the page.

**Uniqueness and effectivity.** The homomorphism is unique because it is
prescribed on the generating set $\{\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}\}$, and it is
computed on a braid word by composing the finitely many automorphisms
$\rho(\sigma_i)^{\pm1}$ attached to its letters, as frozen in
[[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]]. No choice principle and no
geometric input are used in the construction; von Dyck's theorem
[[thm-von-dyck]] supplies existence and uniqueness of the extension.
items.proof_strategy: Apply [[thm-von-dyck]] to the presentation of the braid group: the generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ are sent to the corresponding Artin automorphisms and the braid-relation lemma shows every relator is mapped to the identity, so the assignment extends uniquely. No choice principle and no geometric input are used.

items.title: The geometric action on meridians is the Artin representation
items.statement: Assume AC. Let $G_n$ be the geometric braid group, $\varphi_n:B_n\to G_n$ the published surjection of [[prop-the-artin-presentation-surjects-onto-geometric-braids]], and $\Psi:G_n\to\operatorname{Mod}(D^2,Q_n;\partial D^2)$ the isomorphism of [[thm-braid-group-is-the-boundary-fixed-mapping-class-group-of-the-punctured-disk]]. Identifying $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$ with $F_n$ by the standard meridians, the automorphism induced by the mapping class $\Psi(\varphi_n(\beta))$ equals $\rho(\beta)$ for every braid word $\beta$. In particular the geometric half twist $\sigma_i$ acts as the Nielsen automorphism of [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]].
items.proof_strategy: For a single half twist use part 2 of the mapping-class theorem: $\Psi(\varphi_n(\sigma_i))$ is the class of the explicit homeomorphism $H_i$ supported in the support disc $U_i$ exchanging $q_i,q_{i+1}$. Push the meridian loops through $H_i$: the meridian of $q_i$ becomes a positively oriented meridian of $q_{i+1}$ (same class), and the meridian $x_{i+1}$ is dragged around $q_i$ so that its class becomes $x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}$; every other meridian is fixed because $H_i$ fixes the corresponding punctures and support. Compare with [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]] and use [[thm-induced-fundamental-group-map-functoriality]] to pass from generators to arbitrary braid words, matching the left-to-right word convention. Consistency check owed at Step 3: the direction of the conjugation must match the chosen stacking convention of the geometric half twist, and the display is adjusted only if the geometric read-off forces it (the algebraic convention then propagates).

items.title: The Artin representation is faithful
items.statement: Assume AC. For every $n\ge1$ the Artin representation $\rho:B_n\to\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ of [[def-the-artin-representation-on-a-free-group]] is injective; equivalently, a braid word acts trivially on $F_n$ only if it represents the trivial braid.
items.proof_strategy: Let $\beta\in B_n$ with $\rho(\beta)=\mathrm{id}$. By the geometric-action proposition, the mapping class $\Psi(\varphi_n(\beta))$ acts as the identity on $\pi_1(D^2\setminus Q_n,d)$; by the trivial-action isotopy lemma it is the identity mapping class. Since $\Psi$ is an isomorphism (published, AC), $\varphi_n(\beta)=1$; by completeness of the Artin presentation (published, AC) $\varphi_n$ is injective, so $\beta=1$. For $n\le1$ both groups are trivial and the assertion is immediate. AC is consumed exactly through the published mapping-class isomorphism, the isotopy lemma and completeness, and is stated in the contract.

items.title: Artin automorphisms permute meridian conjugacy classes and fix the boundary word
items.statement: For every braid word $\beta$ and every $i$, $\rho(\beta)(x_i)$ is conjugate in $F_n$ to one of the generators $x_1,\dots,x_n$, and $\rho(\beta)(x_1x_2\cdots x_n)=x_1x_2\cdots x_n$; here $x_1\cdots x_n$ is the boundary word, i.e. the element represented by $\partial$ by [[lem-the-oriented-boundary-loop-represents-the-ordered-product-of-the-standard-meridians]]. No choice principle is used.
items.proof_strategy: Check on the generators: $\rho(\sigma_i)$ sends $x_i$ to $x_{i+1}$ and $x_{i+1}$ to the conjugate $x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}$ of $x_i$, fixing the other generators, and it fixes the ordered product because the two changed letters cancel: $$x_{i+1}\cdot x_{i+1}^{-1}x_ix_{i+1}=x_ix_{i+1}$$ in the free group. Both properties are preserved by composition and by inversion (conjugacy class is a class property; the ordered product is fixed), so they hold for every braid word. The geometric identification of the word $x_1\cdots x_n$ with the boundary loop is the boundary-word lemma.

items.title: Peripheral-boundary-preserving automorphisms of F_n
items.statement:
Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let
$F_n=\langle x_1,\dots,x_n\rangle$ be the free group of [[def-free-group]] on
the $n$ letters $x_1,\dots,x_n$, with reduced words and free reduction as in
[[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]]. The **ordered boundary product** is
the element
$$\delta:=x_1x_2\cdots x_n\in F_n,$$
the word $x_1\cdots x_n$; under the identification of $x_i$ with the class of
the standard meridian of [[def-standard-meridians-of-a-punctured-disk]] it is
the element represented by the positively oriented boundary loop (proved in
`lem-the-oriented-boundary-loop-represents-the-ordered-product-of-the-standard-meridians`).

An automorphism $A\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$
([[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]) is
**peripheral-boundary-preserving** if

1. **(peripheral)** for every $i$ the element $A(x_i)$ is conjugate in $F_n$
   to one of the generators $x_1,\dots,x_n$; equivalently, after rewriting
   $A(x_i)$ in the reduced normal form of
   [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]], there are a permutation $\pi$ of
   $\{1,\dots,n\}$ and a reduced word $Q_i$ with
   $$A(x_i)=Q_i^{-1}\,x_{\pi(i)}\,Q_i;\qquad\text{and}$$
2. **(boundary-preserving)** $A$ fixes the ordered boundary product,
   $$A(x_1x_2\cdots x_n)=x_1x_2\cdots x_n .$$

These are exactly the two hypotheses of Artin's characterization of the braid
subgroup of $\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$.

**The two formulations of condition 1 agree.** If
$A(x_i)=Q_i^{-1}x_{\pi(i)}Q_i$, its class in the abelianisation
$F_n^{\mathrm{ab}}\cong\mathbb Z^n$ is the class of $x_{\pi(i)}$; conversely,
an automorphism induces an automorphism of $\mathbb Z^n$, so if every
$A(x_i)$ is conjugate to a generator, the assignment
$e_i\mapsto e_{\pi(i)}$ is an invertible self-map of the basis and $\pi$ is a
permutation. The element $Q_i$ is not unique, but it is unique up to
left-multiplication by powers of the middle generator: if
$Q^{-1}x_jQ=R^{-1}x_jR$ then $RQ^{-1}$ commutes with $x_j$, hence lies in the
centraliser $\langle x_j\rangle$, so $R=x_j^mQ$ for some integer $m$; thus the invariant content of condition 1 is
"$A(x_i)$ is conjugate to a generator", and the displayed form is a normalised
way of writing that conjugacy. Condition 2 fixes the ordered product itself,
not merely its conjugacy class or its image in the abelianisation. No choice
principle is used in this definition.
items.proof_strategy: This is a definition, not a claim: spell out that condition (i) is invariant under the choice of the conjugating reduced word $Q_i$ up to multiplication by powers of the middle generator, so that 'conjugate to a generator' is the invariant content, and that condition (ii) fixes the ordered product exactly, not merely its conjugacy class. No choice principle is used. Show also that the two formulations agree: an automorphism of $F_n$ induces an automorphism of the abelianisation $\mathbb Z^n$, so if every $A(x_i)$ is conjugate to a generator then the induced map $e_i\mapsto e_{\pi(i)}$ is invertible and $\pi$ is a permutation; conversely the displayed form makes the conjugacy condition immediate.

items.title: Artin's product-cancellation dichotomy
items.statement: Let $A$ be a peripheral-boundary-preserving automorphism ([[def-peripheral-boundary-preserving-automorphism-of-f-n]]) with $A(x_i)=Q_i^{-1}x_{\pi(i)}Q_i$ written in reduced form and $A(x_1\cdots x_n)=x_1\cdots x_n$. Then exactly one of the following holds: (1) in the product $\prod_i Q_i^{-1}x_{\pi(i)}Q_i$ no cancellation between adjacent factors reaches the middle letter $x_{\pi(i)}$ of any factor; then every $Q_i$ is trivial and $\pi$ is the identity, so $A=\mathrm{id}$; (2) some cancellation between two adjacent factors reaches the middle letter of one of them; the first middle letter reached is well defined, and the two affected factors are adjacent in the product.
items.proof_strategy: Substitute and reduce. Since each factor $Q_i^{-1}x_{\pi(i)}Q_i$ is reduced, any cancellation in the product occurs between an initial segment of $Q_i^{-1}$ and the terminal segment of the preceding factor, or analogously for the other side. Case (1): if no middle letter is reached, the surviving residues $R_i$ satisfy $R_1\cdots R_n=x_1\cdots x_n$ with no further cancellation; by uniqueness of reduced words each $R_i$ is a single basis letter, and since $R_i$ contains the middle letter of its factor, the middle letter is $x_i$ in order; then the uncancelled conjugator factors vanish successively from the outside in, giving $Q_i=1$ and $\pi=\mathrm{id}$. Case (2): if a middle letter is reached, record the two adjacent factors and the first middle letter reached (a finite computation: count from both ends of the product toward the first collision). Prove the two cases exhaust all possibilities by uniqueness of free reduction.

items.title: An extremal cancellation shortens an Artin substitution
items.statement: In case (2) of [[lem-artins-product-cancellation-dichotomy]] let $i$ be the smaller of the two adjacent indices and let the first middle letter reached lie in the factor of index $k\in\{i,i+1\}$. Then pre- or post-composition by the Artin automorphism $\rho(\sigma_i)^{\pm1}$ of [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]] replaces the two affected conjugators by residues whose total reduced length is strictly smaller, the composite is again peripheral-boundary-preserving, and it still fixes the ordered product; explicitly $A':=A\circ\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}$ in the alternative where the middle letter of the left factor is reached first, and $A':=\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}\circ A$ in the other, with the inverse formula $\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_i)=x_ix_{i+1}x_i^{-1}$, $\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}(x_{i+1})=x_i$.
items.proof_strategy: Follow Artin's proof of Theorem 16, cases 2(a) and 2(b) (printed pp. 114-115): write the two adjacent reduced factors $Q^{-1}x_aQ$ and $R^{-1}x_bR$ and compute both composites $A\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}$ and $\rho(\sigma_i)^{-1}A$ on the affected generators. The cancellation runs into the middle letter from one side; stopping at the first middle letter leaves strictly shorter remnants which are again conjugates of generators (write the new conjugators explicitly in both alternatives), and the total length of the conjugators decreases. Verify peripheral form is preserved on every generator and that the ordered product is still fixed; print both formulas and the inverse substitution as in the source.

items.title: Every peripheral-boundary-preserving automorphism is an Artin automorphism
items.statement: Every peripheral-boundary-preserving automorphism $A\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ ([[def-peripheral-boundary-preserving-automorphism-of-f-n]]) equals $\rho(\beta)$ for some braid word $\beta$, and $\beta$ may be chosen as a product of the generators $\sigma_1^{\pm1},\dots,\sigma_{n-1}^{\pm1}$. No choice principle is used.
items.proof_strategy: Induct on the total reduced length of the conjugators $Q_i$ chosen as short as possible. If the length is zero, the dichotomy shows $A=\mathrm{id}=\rho(1)$. Otherwise the dichotomy and the shortening lemma give an adjacent index $i$ and a sign such that $A= A'\circ\rho(\sigma_i)$ or $A=\rho(\sigma_i)\circ A'$ with $A'$ peripheral-boundary-preserving of strictly smaller length; by induction $A'=\rho(\beta')$, and since $\rho$ is a homomorphism ([[def-the-artin-representation-on-a-free-group]]) $A=\rho(\beta'\sigma_i^{\pm1})$ or $\rho(\sigma_i^{\pm1}\beta')$. The induction terminates by well-ordering of nonnegative integer lengths and tracks the induced permutation at each step. Note: no completeness or faithfulness is used, so this item is choice-free; the same argument works verbatim for subsets of generators in natural order (Artin's remark).

items.title: Artin's characterization of the braid subgroup of Aut(F_n)
items.statement: Assume AC. The image of the Artin representation $\rho:B_n\to\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ is exactly the set of peripheral-boundary-preserving automorphisms of [[def-peripheral-boundary-preserving-automorphism-of-f-n]]; moreover $\rho$ is injective, so each peripheral-boundary-preserving automorphism is $\rho(\beta)$ for a unique braid $\beta$.
items.proof_strategy: Necessity is the conjugation/boundary-word lemma applied to every braid word. Sufficiency is the previous theorem. Injectivity is faithfulness [[thm-the-artin-representation-is-faithful]] (AC). For $n\le1$ both sides are trivial and the statement is checked directly.

items.title: The Artin action solves the braid word problem
items.statement: Assume AC. Given two words in $\sigma_1^{\pm1},\dots,\sigma_{n-1}^{\pm1}$, the braids they represent are equal if and only if the corresponding automorphisms of $F_n$ agree on the generators $x_1,\dots,x_n$. Since reduced words in a free group are unique and effectively computable, the word problem in $B_n$ is solvable. No choice principle beyond AC is used.
items.proof_strategy: If the braids are equal then the automorphisms are equal because $\rho$ is a well-defined homomorphism; conversely if the automorphisms agree then their quotient is trivial and injectivity of $\rho$ (faithfulness, AC) gives equality of the braids. To decide the comparison, compute the $n$ reduced images (finite words) using [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]] letter by letter and the uniqueness of reduced words of [[thm-reduced-words-form-the-free-group]].

title: The Artin Action on a Free Group — Examples

items.title: The Artin action of the B_3 generators
items.statement: In $B_3$ the two Artin automorphisms of [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]] act by $\rho(\sigma_1): x_1\mapsto x_2$, $x_2\mapsto x_2^{-1}x_1x_2$, $x_3\mapsto x_3$ and $\rho(\sigma_2): x_1\mapsto x_1$, $x_2\mapsto x_3$, $x_3\mapsto x_3^{-1}x_2x_3$. Tabulate both on a basis of $F_3$ and verify the relation $\rho(\sigma_1)\rho(\sigma_2)\rho(\sigma_1)=\rho(\sigma_2)\rho(\sigma_1)\rho(\sigma_2)$ by direct substitution and free reduction.
items.proof_strategy: Substitute the displayed formulas in the six-fold composites and reduce the images of $x_1,x_2,x_3$: both sides send $x_1\mapsto x_3$, $x_2\mapsto x_3^{-1}x_1x_3$, $x_3\mapsto x_3^{-1}x_2^{-1}x_1x_2x_3$, so equality holds on the basis and hence as automorphisms (universal property of the free group).

items.title: The full twist acts by boundary conjugation
items.statement: Let $\Delta^2:=(\sigma_1\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_{n-1})^n\in B_n$ and $\delta:=x_1x_2\cdots x_n\in F_n$. Then $\rho(\Delta^2)(x_i)=\delta^{-1}x_i\delta$ for every $i$; in particular the full twist acts by conjugation by the boundary word.
items.proof_strategy: Compute $\rho(\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_{n-1})$ on the basis: it sends $x_1\mapsto x_2\mapsto\cdots\mapsto x_n$ and $x_i\mapsto \delta_i^{-1}x_{i-1}\delta_i$ for suitable prefixes $\delta_i$; taking the $n$-th power gives $x_i\mapsto\delta^{-1}x_i\delta$ (check the induction from $i$ to $i+1$ explicitly, with the empty-prefix and $i=n$ boundaries). Left-to-right word order and the inverse formulas of [[def-artin-automorphisms-of-the-free-group]] are used throughout.

items.title: A conjugate-permuting automorphism that does not fix the boundary word is not in the braid image
items.statement: For $n\ge2$ let $\varepsilon\in\operatorname{Aut}(F_n)$ be $\varepsilon(x_1)=x_2$, $\varepsilon(x_2)=x_1$, $\varepsilon(x_j)=x_j$ for $j\ge3$. Then $\varepsilon(x_i)$ is conjugate (indeed equal) to a generator for every $i$, but $\varepsilon(x_1x_2\cdots x_n)=x_2x_1x_3\cdots x_n\ne x_1x_2\cdots x_n$; hence $\varepsilon$ is not in the image of the Artin representation. No choice principle is used.
items.proof_strategy: Extend the basis transposition to an involutive free-group automorphism. It preserves positive peripheral classes and changes the ordered product by reduced-word uniqueness; the choice-free Artin necessary direction excludes it from the image. For the reverse nonimplication explicitly compute the involution A(x_1)=x_1^{-1}, A(x_2)=x_1^2x_2, fixing the other letters: A(delta)=delta, while the exponent homomorphism to Z detects that A(x_1) is not conjugate to a positive basis generator. Both witnesses use no choice principle.

items.title: The induced permutation does not determine a braid
items.statement: In $B_3$, the identity and the pure braid word $\sigma_1^2$ induce the same permutation of the punctures (the trivial one), but $\rho(\sigma_1^2)(x_1)=x_2^{-1}x_1x_2\ne x_1$, so they act differently on $F_3$ and are distinct braids. Hence the endpoint permutation of a braid does not determine the braid. The argument uses no choice principle.
items.proof_strategy: Compute $\rho(\sigma_1^2)(x_1)=\rho(\sigma_1)(x_2)=x_2^{-1}x_1x_2$, which is not the reduced word $x_1$; hence $\rho(\sigma_1^2)\ne\mathrm{id}$ while $\rho(1)=\mathrm{id}$, so $\sigma_1^2\ne1$ as braids already at the level of the well-defined homomorphism (no faithfulness needed). Both entries have trivial endpoint permutation: the composition of the geometric surjection with the endpoint permutation sends $\sigma_1\mapsto(1\,2)$, so $\sigma_1^2\mapsto(1\,2)^2=1$, and the identity certainly maps to $1$.
